interviewQuestions.question: Design semantic search over a company's internal documents.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by naming the actual problem: internal docs get phrased inconsistently — different authors describe the same policy differently — so pure keyword search misses a lot of genuinely relevant matches. The fix is embeddings: run every document (chunked into passages, since embedding models have a length limit) through an embedding model, storing the resulting vectors in a vector index alongside a reference back to the source document.

At query time, I'd embed the user's query with the same model and run an approximate nearest-neighbor search (HNSW, typically) to find the closest passage vectors, then return the source documents ranked by similarity.

I'd immediately flag the exact-match gap this creates: if someone searches for a specific policy number or document ID, pure vector search may serve them worse than keyword search would have. So I'd design it as hybrid from the start — run a keyword query alongside the vector query and merge/re-rank the combined results, rather than betting everything on embeddings.

I'd close on freshness: new or edited documents need their embeddings recomputed and re-indexed, which is the same sync-pipeline problem as any other search index, just with an embedding step in front.

**Testing:** whether you can design the vector pipeline end-to-end and still remember exact-match queries need a fallback.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Designing semantic search over documents

interviewQuestions.question: What's an embedding, and why does distance between two embeddings mean something?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd define it concretely: an embedding is a fixed-length vector of numbers — often hundreds to a couple thousand dimensions — produced by a model trained so that inputs with similar meaning end up positioned close together in that vector space, and dissimilar inputs end up far apart. The model learns this positioning from patterns across huge amounts of text (or images), not from any explicit rule a human wrote.

I'd explain the distance computation itself is ordinary math — cosine similarity or Euclidean distance between two number lists — so "how similar are these two pieces of text" becomes a numeric comparison instead of a set intersection over shared words, which is what makes matching by meaning rather than by literal term possible at all.

I'd add the honest caveat: embeddings are only as good as the model that produced them — a model trained on general web text may not capture domain-specific meaning well (medical or legal jargon, for instance) without fine-tuning.

**Testing:** whether you can explain embeddings mechanically, not just wave at "AI understands meaning."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: What embeddings actually are

interviewQuestions.question: How would you decide between a dedicated vector database and adding a vector index to a system you already run?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it as a build-vs-extend trade-off. A dedicated vector database (Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus) is purpose-built around ANN indexing, embedding storage, and metadata filtering, and tends to be more optimized for pure vector workloads at scale. Adding a vector index to an existing store — pgvector on Postgres, `dense_vector` in Elasticsearch — avoids standing up an entirely new system and lets vector similarity combine naturally with the relational or full-text features already in use.

I'd default to the bolt-on option unless vector search is genuinely the core of the product: most applications need vector search as one feature among several (alongside structured filters, keyword search, existing data relationships), and running a whole separate database for it adds real operational cost — another system to secure, back up, and keep in sync.

I'd flag the one case I'd reach for a dedicated vector database anyway: very large-scale, latency-sensitive vector search where the bolt-on option's ANN implementation genuinely can't keep up, which is a real but less common situation than teams initially assume.

**Testing:** whether you weigh operational cost against actual scale needs rather than defaulting to the newest specialized tool.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Dedicated vector DB vs bolt-on vector index
